title: Munchausen syndrome mimicking refractory subcutaneous abscess with bacteremia, diagnosed by repetitive element sequence-based polymerase chain reaction: a case report
case_prompt:
A 24-year-old Japanese woman presented with recurrent fever and subcutaneous abscesses of the left forearm. She was previously healthy and worked as a nurse. Over the prior year she had multiple left-arm abscesses following orthopedic surgeries; for 3 months before admission, abscesses developed repeatedly at sites of blood draws and arterial punctures. Sequential courses of cefazolin, cefotiam, piperacillin–tazobactam, clindamycin, ceftazidime, gentamicin, and meropenem failed to resolve worsening cellulitis, and she developed bacteremia. One week before transfer she underwent incision and drainage.

She had no underlying disease, no psychiatric history, and no social stressors. On admission: T 37.4 °C, BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 70 bpm, RR 15 /min. Examination identified two incisions on the left upper arm with surrounding redness, swelling, and induration; no other infectious foci.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 8400/µL, CRP 2.63 mg/dL, ESR 44.9 mm/h, mild elevation of liver enzymes, normal immunoglobulins, complement levels, neutrophil function tests, and negative HIV. Whole-body contrast CT, transesophageal echocardiography, MRI of the heart and spine, and bone marrow biopsy found no other source of infection. Wound cultures grew Streptococcus mitis, β-Streptococcus, Mobiluncus spp., and Prevotella buccae; blood cultures were initially negative.

She was treated with IV meropenem and linezolid, with prompt resolution, but then developed sudden high fever and severe left-arm pain. Urgent fasciotomy released pus from the supinator muscle. Antibiotics were switched to garenoxacin; Stenotrophomonas maltophilia was later isolated from blood and pus, prompting addition of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (discontinued for allergy) then minocycline. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was administered nine times. Just as discharge was being considered, high fever and a new subcutaneous abscess recurred at the same site.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Treatment failure or inadequate therapy was considered — “We hypothesized that either the treatment had been insufficient or that she had a primary or secondary immune disorder as an underlying disease.”  
2. Local limb predisposition (lymphatic or vascular compromise, dermatophyte co-infection) was considered — “she did not have any disorder affecting the function of her left arm, such as lymphedema due to axillary lymph node dissection or venous insufficiency, peripheral arterial disease, or co-infection with other pathogens such as dermatophytes.”  
3. Secondary immunodeficiency (e.g., diabetes, HIV) was considered — “She showed no signs of underlying secondary immune disorders such as diabetes mellitus or HIV infection.”  
4. Primary immunodeficiency (neutrophil defects) was considered — “we considered the possibility of neutrophil defects, but found no evidence to support this idea (Table 1).”  
5. Atypical fungal or multidrug-resistant bacterial infection was considered — “microbial examinations for fungus and multidrug-resistant bacteria were also conducted but failed to identify the cause.”  
6. Self-inflicted infection (factitious disorder) was considered — “multiple species, including oral indigenous bacteria with a polymicrobial pattern, were detected in cultures of blood and the wound abscess … we finally suspected the possibility of self-injury.”
